samples.text:
The table shows how many doctors and nurses there was for every 10,000 people in six countries in 2010 and 2022.

Overall, most countries had more doctors and nurses in 2022 than in 2010, and in all countries there were more nurses than doctors.

Country A had the most doctors, 38 in 2010 and 45 in 2022. Country E was also high, it increased from 33 to 41. Country B had 26 and 28 doctors. On the other hand, Country C, D and F had few doctors. Country C rose from 11 to 19, Country D from 6 to 9 and Country F had only 2 and then 3.

For nurses, Country A was again the highest with 110 in 2010 and 118 in 2022. Country E increased a lot from 79 to 104. Country B was the only country where the number of nurses go down, from 85 to 81. Country C and Country D also increase, from 25 to 40 and 14 to 30. Country F was the lowest again with 8 and 11 nurses.
samples.why: Relevant overview and accurate figures · doctors and nurses covered separately in a list-like way · linking mechanical · adequate but repetitive vocabulary · agreement and tense errors plus a comma splice, meaning still clear.

samples.text:
The table compares the number of doctors and nurses per 10,000 people in six countries in 2010 and 2022.

Overall, nurses outnumbered doctors in every country in both years, and the provision of health workers generally improved over the period. Country A had the highest ratios and Country F the lowest.

In terms of doctors, Country A led in both years, with the figure rising from 38 to 45, followed closely by Country E, which went from 33 to 41. Country B's figure increased only slightly from 26 to 28. The other three countries had much lower ratios: Country C improved from 11 to 19, while Country D and Country F had fewer than ten doctors per 10,000 people in both years.

The number of nurses was considerably higher. Country A again had the most, at 110 in 2010 and 118 in 2022, while Country E saw the biggest increase, from 79 to 104. Country B was the only country where the ratio of nurses declined, falling from 85 to 81. Meanwhile, the figure for Country D more than doubled from 14 to 30, and Country C also rose significantly to 40, although Country F remained lowest, with just 11.
samples.why: Clear overview of the doctor–nurse gap and extremes · key changes highlighted, including the one decline · good cohesion and some less common vocabulary · mostly error-free with a missing article.

samples.text:
The table presents the number of doctors and nurses per 10,000 people in six countries, comparing figures for 2010 and 2022.

Two features are immediately apparent: nurses outnumbered doctors in every country in both years, and staffing levels improved almost everywhere over the period. There was, however, a striking gap between the best-provided countries, A and E, and the least well-provided, D and F.

Country A had the highest density of both professions, with doctors increasing from 38 to 45 and nurses from 110 to 118. Country E, although slightly behind, recorded the largest absolute gain in nurses, a rise of 25 to reach 104. Country B, by contrast, saw almost no change in its doctor ratio (26 to 28), and it was the only country in which nurse numbers fell, from 85 to 81.

At the lower end, Country C made notable progress, with its doctor ratio climbing from 11 to 19 and its nurse ratio from 25 to 40. Country D more than doubled its nurses from 14 to 30, although it still had only 9 doctors per 10,000 people in 2022. Country F remained far behind the rest, with just 3 doctors and 11 nurses per 10,000 people by the end of the period.
samples.why: Clear two-part overview · countries grouped by level of provision with key contrasts selected · cohesion managed skilfully · precise vocabulary (absolute gain, best-provided) · wide range of structures, error-free.
